transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. Well, I guess the main reason I’m here... it's really been affecting my work, and honestly, it's just getting exhausting. I’m a health services manager, so I oversee operations for a few different clinics, and it's a busy job with a lot of moving parts. But the thing is, anything that takes real, you know, sitting-down brain work... it just feels like I hit a massive brick wall. 

Like, I have these monthly reports I have to do. They're critical. If I don't do them, the whole regional office gets on my case and it messes up our funding metrics. Or, for instance, when I have to plan a multi-site health event, which means coordinating staff, figuring out the logistics for three different locations, looking at schedules... I just keep putting it off. I know it matters. I know exactly what's at stake and how important it is for the clinics, but I will literally do anything else. I'll go check the inventory in the supply closet, or I'll reorganize my desk drawers, or I'll walk around talking to the front desk staff—just to avoid sitting down and doing that heavy mental lifting. 

It’s like my brain just absolutely refuses to engage with it. And the guilt is terrible, because I worked hard for my associate's degree, I worked my way up to this management position, and I *know* I'm capable of the work. But when it comes to actually sitting at my desk and pushing through those big, complex tasks, I just avoid it until the absolute last possible second. It's just a wall I can't seem to climb over anymore.
Looking back at your life, did you experience these same kinds of struggles with focusing on tasks or avoiding work when you were in elementary or middle school?

Oh, absolutely. Yes, it's not a new thing at all, though I think the stakes are just higher now with my job. But back then? Oh boy. If you look back at my elementary school years, it was always the exact same story. Every single parent-teacher conference, it was like a broken record. 

My teachers—especially Mrs. Gable in fourth grade, I still remember her, she had this very stern way of looking over her glasses—she'd tell my parents, "He's such a bright boy, he really has a lot of potential, but he's just always daydreaming." And it was true. I'd be staring out the window at the playground, or looking at the clock, or just completely lost in my own world while everyone else was doing their multiplication tables or reading silently. 

And the worksheets! I don't know how many worksheets I lost between the teacher's desk and my own desk. It was like a black hole in my cubby. I'd do the work sometimes, or at least start it, but then I'd just lose the paper. Or I'd shove it in my backpack and it would get all crumpled up at the bottom under my gym clothes and old permission slips. 

Honestly, the only reason I ever passed or turned anything in was because of my mother. She was a saint, really. Every single night, right after dinner—usually around 6:30, after we'd cleared the kitchen table—she would sit me down and physically empty my entire backpack. She had to check every single folder, every pocket, because if she didn't, I would just completely forget to turn my homework in. Even if I had actually managed to finish the assignment, which was a whole other battle of her sitting there making sure I didn't wander off to play with my dog or turn on the TV, I'd still forget to hand it to the teacher the next morning unless she put it right in the front of my binder. So yeah, it's been this exact same struggle for as long as I can remember, just... manifested differently back then, you know? It's just exhausting to think about how long I've been fighting this same exact battle.
